plants.notes: Ficus villosa is distinguished by its hairy leaves, which press flat to bark in the juvenile [[shingling]] phase. High [[humidity]] helps keep the leaf hairs clean and healthy. It's more tolerant of lower humidity than other ficus but still does best in a closed environment.
plants.toxicity: Ficus sap (a milky latex) can irritate skin and mucous membranes; ingestion may cause mild digestive upset. Toxic to cats and dogs.

plants.nativeContext: Ficus punctata is a [[shingling]]/[[climbing]] fig from Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines) that grows epiphytically on tree trunks in humid [[tropical]] rainforest. Its juvenile leaves press flat to bark and are punctuated with small dot-like structures, giving it its name.
plants.notes: Ficus punctata is a fast-[[shingling]] background [[vine]] once established, capable of creating a dense covering on backgrounds. It needs a vertical surface, high [[humidity]], and [[bright-indirect|bright indirect light]] for best growth. It produces waxy, pale green juvenile leaves with interesting texture.
plants.toxicity: Ficus sap (a milky latex) can irritate skin and mucous membranes; ingestion may cause mild digestive upset. Toxic to cats and dogs.

plants.nativeContext: Ficus pumila 'Snowflake' is a variegated [[cultivar]] of the [[creeping]] fig, native to East Asia. The species climbs walls and tree trunks by means of adhesive root pads. The 'Snowflake' cultivar features irregular cream-white splashes and margins on its small rounded leaves.
plants.notes: Ficus pumila 'Snowflake' is one of the most manageable [[shingling]] figs for terrariums, more tolerant of temperature variation and lower [[humidity]] than [[tropical]] species. It grows vigorously once established, so trim it regularly.
plants.toxicity: Ficus sap (a milky latex) can irritate skin and mucous membranes; ingestion may cause mild digestive upset. Toxic to cats and dogs.

plants.nativeContext: Micranthemum tweedei, sold under the trade name 'Monte Carlo', is native to Argentina and Uruguay where it grows as a semi-[[aquatic]] carpet plant along stream margins and seasonally inundated areas. It is popular in aquascaping and emersed terrarium work.
plants.notes: Micranthemum tweedei, commonly known as Monte Carlo, forms a dense, low bright-green carpet when grown in high-[[humidity]] terrariums. It needs a nutrient-rich fine substrate kept permanently saturated, making it excellent for the floor of a high-humidity closed build. Under bright light it stays compact; under [[low|low light]], stems [[etiolation|etiolate]] and the carpet opens up.

plants.nativeContext: Anoectochilus albolineatus is a jewel [[orchid]] native to the humid understorey of [[tropical]] Southeast Asian forests, from peninsular Malaysia through to Borneo and Sumatra. It grows on damp, leaf-littered forest floors in deep shade, producing velvety dark leaves with striking white or silver veining.
plants.notes: Anoectochilus albolineatus is a jewel [[orchid]] grown primarily for its foliage rather than its flowers. Plant it in a shallow layer of fine-grade sphagnum or sphagnum-[[peat]] mix and maintain high, stable [[humidity]] without wetting the leaves directly. Rotting stems are the main failure mode — good air circulation is essential to prevent stagnant conditions despite the humidity, and the plant is very rewarding once it stabilizes.

plants.nativeContext: Anoectochilus formosanus is the Taiwanese jewel [[orchid]], endemic to Taiwan's humid mountain forests at elevations of 500–2000 m. It has a long history in Chinese traditional medicine and is one of the more cold-tolerant Anoectochilus species.
plants.notes: Anoectochilus formosanus, the Formosan Jewel [[orchid|Orchid]], is one of the easier species in the genus to maintain. Keep it in sphagnum with stable moisture and indirect light. It's widely available and a good introduction to jewel orchid cultivation.

plants.nativeContext: Masdevallia auropurpurea is a cool-growing [[epiphytic]] [[orchid]] from the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador, typically found at elevations of 1800–2800 m. It produces dramatic flowers with gold-yellow inner coloration and purple-flushed sepaline tails.
plants.notes: Masdevallia auropurpurea is a cool-growing [[orchid]] that critically requires cool temperatures — sustained warmth above 22°C will kill it. A [[closed-terrarium|closed terrarium]] will overheat unless actively chilled, so it's best grown in a cool-room terrarium with excellent ventilation. Plant it in fine bark-sphagnum mix and never let the roots dry completely. Distilled or other pure water is important for this genus.

plants.nativeContext: Masdevallia floribunda is a compact, free-flowering cool-to-intermediate growing [[orchid]] from the cloud forests of Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras at 1200–2500 m elevation. As the name suggests, it produces an abundance of small, delicate flowers throughout the year.
plants.notes: Masdevallia floribunda is one of the more tolerant Masdevallia species and slightly more adaptable than most. It needs good air movement, consistently moist fine bark or sphagnum, and cool to intermediate temperatures. A cool, well-ventilated [[open-terrarium|open terrarium]] or an [[orchid]] case suits it well; it will not tolerate stagnant warm air.

plants.nativeContext: Masdevallia nidifica is a cool-growing miniature [[orchid]] from the high cloud forests of Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, and Ecuador at 1600–2800 m. The name 'nidifica' refers to the nest-like cluster of leaves. It produces small but charming pale flowers with elongated tails.
plants.notes: Masdevallia nidifica is a true cool-grower that suffers in any warmth above 22°C. It requires near-constant high [[humidity]] with outstanding air movement. It can be mounted on cork bark or grown in a well-vented [[open-terrarium|open terrarium]]; its miniature size makes it ideal where space is limited but temperatures permit.

plants.nativeContext: Pleurothallis grobyi is one of the most widespread and vigorous miniature [[orchid|orchids]], ranging from Mexico and the Caribbean through Central America to Bolivia and Brazil. It adapts well to intermediate conditions, making it one of the easier Pleurothallis species for beginners.
plants.notes: Pleurothallis grobyi is one of the most beginner-friendly miniature [[orchid|orchids]], tolerating a wider temperature range than most Pleurothallis and growing vigorously once settled. It produces bright yellow-orange tiny flowers in clusters throughout the year, making it an excellent starter species for a high-[[humidity]] terrarium.

plants.nativeContext: Pleurothallis rubella is a miniature [[epiphytic]] [[orchid]] from the cloud forests of Central and South America. It grows in perpetually moist, shaded conditions and produces small reddish-pink flowers that appear from the leaf surface throughout the year.
plants.notes: Pleurothallis rubella is a small terrarium [[orchid]] suited to cool to intermediate conditions, with a reddish tint in the leaves and flowers that gives it distinctive appeal in a terrarium. Keep the roots moist on a cork or bark mount and ensure good airflow to prevent rot. Avoid temperature extremes.

plants.nativeContext: Restrepia lansburgii is a cool-to-intermediate growing [[epiphytic]] [[orchid]] from the Andes cloud forests of Colombia and Venezuela, found at 1500–2800 m elevation. Restrepia species produce a succession of colorful, intricate flowers from the leaf base throughout the year.
plants.notes: Restrepia lansburgii is an excellent candidate for a well-ventilated cool [[orchid]] terrarium — it stays compact and flowers continuously when conditions are right. Provide intermediate to cool temperatures (12–22°C), good airflow, and consistent moisture without waterlogging. It will not tolerate the heat of a closed tropics-style [[vivarium]].

plants.nativeContext: Restrepia muscifera is a cool-growing Andean cloud forest [[orchid]] from Colombia, Venezuela, and Ecuador at 1500–2700 m. The name 'muscifera' (fly-bearing) refers to the fly-mimicking flower structure it uses to attract insect pollinators.
plants.notes: Restrepia muscifera prefers intermediate to cool temperatures, high [[humidity]], and excellent air circulation. Its patterned flowers mimic flies, and it produces flowers at multiple times of year from leaf [[node|nodes]]. An ideal cool-case [[orchid]] for a specimen [[vivarium]].

plants.nativeContext: Scaphosepalum dodsoni is a miniature cool-growing [[orchid]] from the cloud forests of Ecuador and Colombia at 1800–2500 m elevation. Scaphosepalum species are known for their unusual asymmetric flowers and their habit of producing blooms in sequence from a single long-lived inflorescence.
plants.notes: Scaphosepalum dodsoni requires cool cloud-forest conditions and should not exceed 22°C. Its single flower spike blooms repeatedly over months, opening one flower at a time. It can be grown mounted or in small pots with excellent drainage and very high [[humidity]] with airflow. This is not a plant for [[tropical]] vivaria; it needs a cool case.

plants.nativeContext: Stelis argentata is a miniature [[epiphytic]] [[orchid]] from the [[montane]] cloud forests of Central and South America, found from Mexico to Bolivia at 1000–2800 m. It produces tiny, intricate flowers arranged in dense rows along slender spikes, often with a silvery sheen.
plants.notes: Stelis argentata is among the most compact and container-friendly of the miniature [[orchid|orchids]]. It can be mounted on cork bark or grown in small pots of fine sphagnum with excellent drainage; intermediate temperatures and good [[humidity]] and airflow suit most collections. It produces flowers multiple times per year.

plants.nativeContext: Bulbophyllum intersitum is a warm-to-intermediate growing [[epiphytic]] [[orchid]] from Southeast Asia's [[tropical]] forests. Like most Bulbophyllum, it grows on mossy tree bark in humid, warm rainforest conditions and produces distinctive, often unusually-shaped flowers.
plants.notes: Bulbophyllum intersitum is a warm-growing species more suited to [[tropical]] vivaria than cool-growing [[orchid|orchids]]. Mount it on cork bark and ensure the [[pseudobulb|pseudobulbs]] and roots never dry out completely between waterings; good [[humidity]] and warmth are the main requirements. The [[pseudobulb|pseudobulbs]] store water, which provides some drought tolerance.

plants.nativeContext: Formerly placed in Cirrhopetalum, now considered Bulbophyllum farreri, this [[orchid]] originates from the Himalayan foothills through to Myanmar and southern China. It grows as an [[epiphyte]] in [[subtropical]] and warm-[[temperate]] forests and produces characteristic umbellate flower clusters with extended lateral sepals.
plants.notes: Bulbophyllum farreri is one of the more temperature-flexible Bulbophyllum relatives, tolerating intermediate to cool-warm conditions. Mount it on a bark slab and allow it to creep freely; keep it consistently moist during growth, and a slight dry rest in cooler months can encourage flowering.

plants.nativeContext: Haraella odorata (sometimes spelled Haerella) is a monotypic miniature [[orchid]] genus endemic to Taiwan. It grows as an [[epiphyte]] in the island's [[subtropical]] and [[montane]] forests, producing a succession of fragrant, yellow-and-purple-striped flowers from a small fan of strap-like leaves.
plants.notes: Haraella odorata is a delightful miniature [[orchid]] — compact enough for small terrariums and surprisingly adaptable. It can be grown on bark mounts or in small baskets with fine sphagnum, and it flowers multiple times per year with a sweet fragrance. It tolerates a range of temperatures from cool [[subtropical]] to warm.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia angulata (syn. P. quadrangularis) is native to the [[tropical]] forests of Central and South America. It grows as a compact, [[trailing]] herb in the humid forest understorey, producing distinctive dark-green leaves with paler longitudinal stripes along the veins.
plants.notes: Peperomia angulata is a robust, low-maintenance terrarium peperomia. Its [[trailing]] stems and striped leaves work well in mid-level positions, and it performs reliably under [[low|low light]], making it useful in darker terrarium corners. Allow the substrate to approach dryness between waterings — peperomia roots rot easily in saturated soil.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia emarginella is a miniature [[creeping]] peperomia native to the cloud forests of the Andes, from Colombia south to Bolivia. It grows as a low herb on mossy rocks and tree bases, producing tiny notched (emarginate) leaves on fine, [[trailing]] red stems.
plants.notes: Peperomia emarginella is an ideal small terrarium peperomia — extremely compact and slow-growing with almost jewel-like tiny leaves that are beautiful for covering the base of [[hardscape]]. Allow the substrate to partially dry between waterings; the small leaf size means it loses moisture quickly if [[humidity]] drops, so keep it in a closed environment.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia guttulata is a South American peperomia with distinctive patterned leaves — typically dark green with pale silver spots or banding. It grows in the humid forest understorey, often on mossy substrate or leaf litter.
plants.notes: Peperomia guttulata is a moderately easy terrarium peperomia with attractive foliar patterning. Allow it to partially dry between waterings, and keep it in [[medium|medium light]] to preserve leaf contrast — [[low|low light]] can reduce the patterning. It suits a mid-layer position in a closed [[tropical]] build.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia puteolata is native to the [[tropical]] forests of Peru and surrounding South America. It produces elongated leaves with multiple parallel pale veins on dark green, the stems arranged in a whorled pattern — one of the most distinctive peperomia species in cultivation.
plants.notes: Peperomia puteolata is one of the easiest peperomia for terrariums. Its whorled, striped foliage provides good visual interest, and it tolerates moderate [[humidity]] rather than requiring saturation. Allow the substrate to partially dry between waterings; it suits both small and large enclosed builds, and periodic trimming keeps it in shape.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia rubella is a miniature [[trailing]] peperomia native to Jamaica's [[montane]] forests. It produces tiny, oval leaves with distinctive reddish-burgundy undersides and stems, growing in a delicate trailing or hanging habit on mossy rocks and tree limbs.
plants.notes: Peperomia rubella is a charming, compact peperomia with red-underside leaves. Avoid heavy watering — the small, fleshy leaves store moisture. The red coloration intensifies in brighter indirect light, and good [[humidity]] helps it stay compact and healthy.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia serpens is a vining peperomia native to the [[tropical]] forests of Central and South America, where its long, snaking stems climb or trail through humid understorey vegetation. It produces heart-shaped, somewhat [[succulent]] leaves on wiry, flexible stems.
plants.notes: Peperomia serpens has a [[trailing]] and [[climbing]] habit that makes it an excellent choice for vertical elements in a [[vivarium]] — its stems will attach loosely to cork bark or wood. Keep it moist but allow intermittent drying to prevent [[root-rot|root rot]]. It grows readily once established; trim back if it becomes too dominant.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia trinervis is a compact peperomia native to [[tropical]] South America and the Caribbean, growing in humid shaded forest floors and on mossy tree bases. Its three-veined leaves are characteristic of the species.
plants.notes: Peperomia trinervis is a reliable, compact terrarium peperomia whose three-veined leaf structure gives it a subtle but appealing texture. Standard peperomia care applies: moderate [[humidity]], allow partial drying between waterings, and avoid cold and waterlogging. It suits smaller closed builds well.

plants.nativeContext: Peperomia verticillata is native to Cuba and the Caribbean, growing in rocky forest habitats. The 'Red Log' [[cultivar]] is notable for its deep crimson-red undersides contrasting with dark green upper leaf surfaces on compact whorled stems — giving a striking bicolor effect.
plants.notes: Peperomia verticillata 'Red Log' is one of the most visually striking peperomia for terrarium with deep red undersides. It prefers slightly lower [[humidity]] than many [[tropical]] terrariums. Allow partial drying between waterings.

plants.nativeContext: Piper crocatum is a [[climbing]] pepper [[vine]] native to Peru, where it grows in the understorey of [[tropical]] and cloud-forest margins. Its leaves are dramatically patterned with pink-to-silver splotches on dark green, with deep red-purple undersides — making it one of the most ornamental [[foliage|foliage plants]] in the genus.
plants.notes: Piper crocatum is an eye-catching terrarium [[vine]] that climbs readily up branches or cork bark. The metallic leaf patterning intensifies under medium to [[bright-indirect|bright indirect light]]; too little light and the coloration fades. Keep it consistently moist without waterlogging, trim it periodically as growth can become vigorous, and avoid cold temperatures.
plants.toxicity: The sap contains irritant compounds; wash hands after handling and avoid touching eyes or mucous membranes.

plants.nativeContext: Sphagnum palustre is a bog [[moss]] widespread across cool [[temperate]] regions of the Northern Hemisphere, forming deep, water-retaining mats in fens, bogs, and humid forest margins.
plants.notes: [[sphagnum|Sphagnum Moss]] is the workhorse of [[closed-terrarium|closed terrariums]] — it retains enormous amounts of water, acidifies its microenvironment, and acts as both substrate and living carpet. Keep it perpetually moist but never waterlogged; it rots if standing water drowns the base. It thrives in [[low|low light]] under a sealed lid and doubles as a moisture indicator: pale and springy means healthy, brown and dense means too dry.

plants.nativeContext: Vesicularia ferriei is a [[tropical]] [[moss]] native to East and Southeast Asia, found growing on shaded, humid rock faces and tree bark near streams and waterfalls.
plants.notes: Weeping [[moss|Moss]] drapes downward in delicate, overlapping [[frond|fronds]] — it is most effective tied to driftwood or cork bark where its pendulous habit can hang freely. It tolerates [[low|low light]] well and stays lush under a closed lid. Keep it moist but not waterlogged; unlike [[aquatic]] mosses it does not need to be submerged.

plants.nativeContext: Lemmaphyllum microphyllum is a miniature [[epiphytic]] [[fern]] from East and Southeast Asia, growing on mossy tree bark and rocks in humid forest environments. It produces tiny, round (coin-shaped) [[frond|fronds]] on [[creeping]] [[rhizome|rhizomes]], carpeting surfaces with a delicate texture.
plants.notes: Lemmaphyllum microphyllum is an excellent [[epiphytic]] terrarium [[fern]] that grows flat against bark or [[moss]] walls, producing a charming mosaic of tiny round fronds. It can be attached to cork bark or grown on moist wood, and it tolerates lower temperatures than many [[tropical]] ferns. Keep it moist and humid — the small [[frond|fronds]] [[desiccate]] quickly if conditions drop.

plants.nativeContext: Pleopeltis percussa is a drought-tolerant [[epiphytic]] [[fern]] from the [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] Americas, growing on tree bark and rocky outcrops. Its strap-shaped [[frond|fronds]] are marked with distinctive impressed dots (punctae) on the surface, from which the common name derives.
plants.notes: Pleopeltis percussa, the Wart [[fern|Fern]], is a tough [[epiphytic]] fern well-suited to terrarium culture. It can survive brief dry periods by curling its [[frond|fronds]] in a manner similar to resurrection ferns, and it rewets readily from dormancy. It can be mounted on bark or grown in a well-draining mix, and it's easier to care for than many of the more delicate terrarium ferns.

plants.nativeContext: Pyrrosia nummularifolia is a miniature [[creeping]] [[epiphytic]] [[fern]] from Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia), producing tiny round, coin-shaped [[frond|fronds]] on creeping [[rhizome|rhizomes]]. It grows on mossy bark in humid [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] forest.
plants.notes: Pyrrosia nummularifolia is a popular terrarium [[fern]] for its miniature, perfectly round [[frond|fronds]] that carpet bark and wood surfaces over time. Keep the [[rhizome|rhizomes]] exposed rather than buried, attach it to cork or a wood panel, and provide moderate to high [[humidity]] and stable warmth for the best growth. It's very slow-growing, but it forms attractive dense mats once established.

plants.nativeContext: Actiniopteris australis is a distinctive [[fern]] from [[arid]] and semi-arid rocky habitats across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. Its fan-shaped, palm-like [[frond|fronds]] are highly adapted to drought, allowing the plant to survive in rock crevices and dry hillsides where most ferns cannot.
plants.notes: Actiniopteris australis, the Palm [[fern|Fern]], is an unusual [[arid]]-adapted fern completely unlike typical terrarium ferns. It's best suited to a dryland or desert [[open-terrarium|open terrarium]] rather than a closed humid build — allow the substrate to dry thoroughly between waterings and provide bright, indirect to partial [[direct|direct light]]. It's very drought-tolerant once established but dislikes overwatering.

plants.nativeContext: Hatiora salicornioides (dancing bones or drunkard's dream) is an [[epiphytic]] cactus native to the humid [[tropical]] Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil. Unlike desert cacti it grows on trees in warm, humid conditions, producing yellow-orange flowers at the tips of small segmented stems.
plants.notes: Hatiora salicornioides, the Dancing Bones Cactus, is a forest [[epiphyte]] that prefers higher [[humidity]] and more water than desert cacti — but still needs good drainage and periodic drying between waterings. It can be mounted on bark or grown in a fast-draining bark-[[perlite]] mix; [[bright-indirect|bright indirect light]] and moderate humidity in an [[open-terrarium|open terrarium]] suit it well. A brief cooler, drier rest period in winter will encourage spring blooming.
plants.toxicity: May cause mild digestive upset (vomiting, diarrhea) if ingested by cats or dogs.

plants.nativeContext: Muehlenbeckia complexa is native to New Zealand and parts of Australia where it forms dense, scrambling tangles of wiry stems across coastal scrub, dunes, and rocky hillsides. Its tiny round leaves on hair-fine, dark stems create an almost [[moss]]-like visual effect at [[scale]].
plants.notes: Muehlenbeckia complexa, the Wire [[vine|Vine]], is one of the easiest [[trailing]] vines for [[open-terrarium|open terrariums]] and desert-style builds. It grows vigorously once established and needs regular trimming to prevent it from dominating an enclosure. It prefers cooler temperatures and lower [[humidity]] than [[tropical]] plants, making it ideal for [[temperate]] or [[mediterranean|Mediterranean]]-style terrariums.
plants.toxicity: The small berries can cause digestive upset if ingested by pets or children; keep flowering or fruiting plants away from curious pets.

plants.nativeContext: A variegated [[cultivar]] of the New Zealand wire [[vine]], with irregular cream, white, or pale-green splashing on the tiny round leaves. The wiry stems remain dark, creating a striking contrast with the light variegation.
plants.notes: Muehlenbeckia complexa 'Variegated' grows more slowly than the standard green form because of its reduced chlorophyll, and it needs more light than the green form to maintain the variegation and grow well. The same cool, [[open-terrarium|open terrarium]] conditions as the species apply: good airflow, allow partial drying, and cool temperatures. Trim it regularly to keep it compact.
plants.toxicity: The small berries can cause digestive upset if ingested by pets or children; keep flowering or fruiting plants away from curious pets.

plants.nativeContext: Selaginella erythropus 'Sanguinea' is a form of the red spike [[moss]] native to the humid [[tropical]] forests of Central and South America. The 'Sanguinea' selection is chosen for its especially vivid blood-red to ruby coloration on the upper [[frond]] surface, contrasting with pale green undersides.
plants.notes: Selaginella erythropus 'Sanguinea' has nice red coloration that is most vivid under low to medium indirect light at high [[humidity]] — unlike many red plants, bright light can actually reduce the color intensity. It can be grown in consistently moist fine [[peat]] or coco-coir and makes excellent [[ground-cover|ground cover]] for [[tropical]] closed builds. High ambient humidity is required.

plants.nativeContext: Selaginella martensii 'Watsoniana' is a [[cultivar]] of a Mexican and Central American spike [[moss]] species, selected for variegated silver-white tips on the [[frond]] ends that give a frosted or snow-dusted appearance to the otherwise green foliage.
plants.notes: Selaginella martensii 'Watsoniana' is an extremely attractive selaginella for closed builds — the silver-tipped [[frond|fronds]] glow under terrarium lighting. It prefers slightly cooler temperatures and lower [[humidity]] than strictly [[tropical]] species, making it more versatile than many selaginellas. Keep it moist at all times; it's a reliable and forgiving [[ground-cover|ground cover]].

plants.nativeContext: Pilea libanensis 'Aquamarine' is a [[cultivar]] of a small Pilea species producing a cloud of delicate, thread-like stems and tiny round leaves with a blue-green to aquamarine tint. It grows as a groundcover in humid [[subtropical]] to [[tropical]] forests.
plants.notes: Pilea libanensis 'Aquamarine' has fine stems and tiny leaves that resemble a miniature cloud or soft [[moss]] from a distance. It prefers moderate to high [[humidity]] and moist but well-drained substrate. Trim it periodically to keep it dense and compact; it suits foreground or mid-level positions.

plants.nativeContext: Pilea pubescens 'Silver Cloud' is a Caribbean and [[tropical]] South American Pilea [[cultivar]] selected for heavily silver-frosted foliage — the metallic sheen covering most of the leaf surface gives the impression of a silver cloud above the green base.
plants.notes: Pilea pubescens 'Silver Cloud' is a striking metallic-leaved pilea well-suited to [[closed-terrarium|closed terrariums]]. The silver coloration is brightest under [[medium|medium light]] — too low and it fades, too high and it bleaches. Keep it moist and humid. It's compact and relatively well-behaved, which makes it a good small terrarium and beginner plant.

plants.nativeContext: Pilea spruceana is native to the cool cloud forests of the Andes in Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia. It grows in intermediate-temperature humid forest understorey, producing deeply textured, chocolate-brown leaves with a contrasting silver metallic sheen running between the raised veins.
plants.notes: Pilea spruceana is one of the most ornamental Pilea species for terrariums, with dramatic texture and silver-on-brown coloration that are most vivid in medium indirect light. It prefers cooler temperatures than typical [[tropical|tropicals]] — 16–24°C is ideal — and the substrate should be allowed to approach partial dryness between waterings to avoid root saturation.

plants.nativeContext: Procris pulchra is a small [[trailing]] herb in the nettle family (Urticaceae) native to humid [[tropical]] forests of Southeast Asia, where it grows on moist rocks, mossy soil, and stream banks in deeply shaded conditions. The leaves are marked with distinctive silver or pale patterning on a dark green base.
plants.notes: Procris pulchra is a rarely cultivated but beautiful terrarium plant with fittonia-like silver patterning on dark leaves. It requires consistently high [[humidity]] and shade — similar conditions to fittonia but even more shade-tolerant — and the substrate should be kept moist at all times. It's a rewarding accent plant for mature, stable [[closed-terrarium|closed terrariums]].

plants.nativeContext: Cissus amazonica is a [[climbing]] [[vine]] native to the rainforests of the Amazon basin in Brazil and neighboring South America. It produces lanceolate, dark-green leaves marked with a distinctive silver chevron pattern along the [[midrib]] and lateral veins, with deep red-purple undersides.
plants.notes: Cissus amazonica is an excellent large-build terrarium [[vine]] with striking metallic foliage that climbs readily on wood, cork, or background panels. Keep it consistently moist with high [[humidity]] — the large leaf area transpires rapidly in dry conditions. Vigorous growth means regular trimming may be needed in enclosed spaces.
plants.toxicity: The sap can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals; wear gloves when pruning or repotting.

plants.nativeContext: Cissus discolor is native to the [[tropical]] forests of Southeast Asia (Java, Borneo, Cambodia), where it grows as a vigorous [[climbing]] [[vine]] in humid forest edges and clearings. Its large leaves display spectacular red, silver, and green iridescent patterning with deep purple undersides — resembling rex [[begonia|begonias]], hence the common name.
plants.notes:
Cissus discolor, the Rex [[begonia|Begonia]] [[vine|Vine]], is one of the most dramatically patterned [[climbing]] plants available for terrariums. It's best suited to large terrariums where its vigorous growth can be accommodated. [[bright-indirect|Bright indirect light]] is needed to maintain the spectacular leaf coloration; keep it moist and trim it regularly, as it will climb aggressively up any support.
